course.title: Identity & Access Management
course.description: A complete, practical Identity & Access Management course covering the lifecycle and security engineering of digital identities. Students learn identity concepts, account governance, authentication and assurance, password security, phishing-resistant MFA, authorization models, RBAC and ABAC, least privilege, separation of duties, SAML and OAuth/OIDC federation, SCIM provisioning, deprovisioning, privileged access, service/workload identity, token and session protection, access reviews, identity monitoring, zero-trust architecture, contextual access policy, and a defensive IAM governance capstone. The course is designed for learners who need both conceptual understanding and practical ability to design, review, and operate IAM controls in enterprise and application environments.
prerequisites: Familiarity with HTTP, JSON, and web applications is helpful.
Basic command-line use is recommended for the capstone but is not required for the conceptual lessons.
learningOutcomes: Explain digital identity, authentication, authorization, federation, provisioning, and lifecycle-management concepts.
Design joiner-mover-leaver processes for human and non-human identities.
Choose authentication methods using assurance, phishing-resistance, and recovery considerations.
Design RBAC and ABAC authorization policies using least privilege and separation of duties.
Explain and safely reason about SAML, OAuth 2.0, OpenID Connect, and SCIM.
Protect sessions, access tokens, privileged accounts, and workload identities.
Design privileged-access and emergency-access controls with monitoring and review.
Create access-review and reconciliation processes that detect identity drift.
Apply zero-trust and contextual access principles to identity-centric architectures.
Build and test a read-only IAM access-governance analyzer and interpret its findings responsibly.

modules.title: Identity Foundations and Lifecycle
modules.description: Build the vocabulary and lifecycle model required to design and operate identity systems safely.

lessons.title: Digital Identity, Subjects, Claims, and Attributes
lessons.description: Learn how digital systems represent subjects, identifiers, attributes, and claims.
learningObjectives: Explain the difference between a subject, identifier, attribute, and claim.
Describe why an identifier does not automatically prove identity.
Model a simple identity record without over-collecting personal data.

notes.text: Identity is contextual

A digital identity is a representation of a subject within a service. An identifier can name the subject, while claims and attributes provide additional information. Authentication establishes control of an authenticator associated with an identity; identity proofing establishes evidence about a real-world subject when that level of assurance is required.

items: Prefer stable internal identifiers over predictable public database keys.
Minimize attributes collected and exposed to relying applications.
Document which claims are authoritative and how recently they were verified.

quiz.question: Which statement best distinguishes an identifier from authentication?
options: An identifier proves the person owns an account
An identifier names a subject; authentication verifies control of an authenticator
An identifier is always personally identifying
quiz.answer: An identifier names a subject; authentication verifies control of an authenticator
quiz.explanation: Names and authentication evidence serve different purposes.

summary: Identity data should be modeled separately from authentication evidence.
Claims need an issuer and context when they cross trust boundaries.

lessons.title: Identity Lifecycle: Joiner, Mover, Leaver
lessons.description: Design account and access changes around the employee or contractor lifecycle.
learningObjectives: Map joiner, mover, and leaver events to identity actions.
Explain why deprovisioning speed matters.
Identify stale-account and orphaned-access risks.

notes.text: Identity lifecycle management connects authoritative personnel or business events to digital access. Joining creates accounts and baseline access; moving changes access when duties change; leaving removes or disables access and retrieves or rotates credentials and tokens as appropriate.

items: Use authoritative sources for employment or supplier status.
Avoid leaving former role memberships attached after a transfer.
Treat shared or service accounts as separate lifecycle objects with owners.

practicals.title: Joiner-Mover-Leaver Access Review
practicals.description: Translate three lifecycle events into additions, removals, approvals, and evidence.
steps: Create fictional joiner, mover, and leaver records.
For each record, list current access and the desired final access.
Mark access to add, remove, or review, and identify the accountable owner.
Record the evidence required to prove the action occurred.
practicals.solution: Example: joiner -> create baseline account and approved role; mover -> remove obsolete role and add new approved role; leaver -> disable account, revoke active sessions/tokens, and review downstream access.
practicals.output: An auditable lifecycle table with access changes, owners, approvals, and evidence.

quiz.question: What is the main security risk when a mover event is not reflected in access systems?
options: Accumulated or inappropriate privileges from the previous role
quiz.answer: Accumulated or inappropriate privileges from the previous role
quiz.explanation: Role changes can leave users with access they no longer need.

summary: Lifecycle automation reduces access drift.
Transfers require removal as well as addition of access.

lessons.title: Account Types: Workforce, External, Service, and Emergency
lessons.description: Differentiate human and non-human account classes and their control needs.
learningObjectives: Classify common account types.
Assign ownership and lifecycle requirements to service accounts.
Design emergency access controls and review expectations.

items: Workforce accounts normally map to a person.
External accounts require sponsor and expiration controls.
Service identities represent software or workloads and should be constrained by purpose.
Emergency or break-glass accounts are exceptional paths requiring stronger monitoring and controlled storage.

notes.text: Do not solve shared-account problems by simply adding more people to one privileged identity. Prefer individually attributable identities plus delegated roles where practical.

quiz.question: Which account type most clearly requires an explicit non-human owner and rotation/credential-management process?
quiz.answer: Service account
quiz.explanation: Non-human identities need accountable ownership and lifecycle management.

summary: Account taxonomy drives appropriate lifecycle controls.
Attribution and ownership are essential for privileged and non-human identities.

lessons.title: Identity Governance and Policy
lessons.description: Connect organizational policy to access standards and reviewable decisions.
learningObjectives: Define identity governance in operational terms.
Translate policy statements into measurable controls.
Identify ownership, evidence, exception, and review requirements.

notes.text: Identity governance defines who may request, approve, receive, use, review, and revoke access. A good policy distinguishes mandatory controls from risk-based exceptions and identifies evidence needed for audit or investigation.

items: Policy should define role ownership and approval authority.
Exceptions require rationale, compensating controls, owner, and review date.
Metrics should measure control effectiveness, not merely the number of accounts.

quiz.question: Which artifact best demonstrates that an access exception is being governed?
options: A hidden spreadsheet with no owner
A documented exception with business rationale, owner, controls, and review date
quiz.answer: A documented exception with business rationale, owner, controls, and review date
quiz.explanation: Governed exceptions are traceable and reviewable.

summary: Governance makes technical access decisions accountable.
Evidence should show how decisions were made, not just the final state.

tasks.title: Design a Joiner-Mover-Leaver Control Matrix
tasks.description: Create a control matrix linking HR events to account and access actions.
tasks.problemStatement: A fictional organization has workforce members changing roles, joining, or leaving. Define the access actions, owners, evidence, and timing expectations for each lifecycle event.
objectives: Map lifecycle events to identity actions.
Define evidence that can be audited.
requirements: Use neutral fictional identities and no real personal data.
tasks.hint: Start with authoritative lifecycle events, then define the minimum digital changes needed.
tasks.solutionCode:
event,identity_action,owner,evidence
joiner,create account and baseline access,identity team,provisioning record
mover,remove old role and grant new approved role,identity + manager,approval and change record
leaver,disable account and revoke sessions/tokens,identity team,deprovisioning record
tasks.solutionExplanation: The matrix separates lifecycle triggers from access operations and identifies accountability and evidence for each transition.

modules.title: Authentication and Assurance
modules.description: Learn authenticators, assurance levels, password security, MFA, phishing resistance, and recovery.

lessons.title: Authentication Factors and Assurance
lessons.description: Understand the categories of authentication factors and why assurance level matters.
learningObjectives: Differentiate knowledge, possession, and inherence factors.
Explain authentication assurance levels at a high level.
Select an authenticator strategy based on threat and assurance needs.

notes.text: Authentication verifies that a claimant controls one or more authenticators bound to an identity. NIST SP 800-63B defines AAL1, AAL2, and AAL3 with increasing requirements for authentication strength, replay resistance, phishing resistance, and hardware protections.

items: AAL is about the authentication process, not the importance of the account by itself.
Riskier systems may need stronger authenticators or additional transaction controls.
Do not confuse identity proofing assurance with authentication assurance.

quiz.question: Which NIST assurance concept specifically measures the strength of the authentication transaction?
quiz.answer: AAL
quiz.explanation: AAL means Authenticator Assurance Level.

summary: Authentication assurance and identity proofing are distinct dimensions.
Choose assurance based on the protected action and threat model.

lessons.title: Passwords and Password Storage
lessons.description: Apply current password-management and password-storage guidance.
learningObjectives: Explain why plaintext password storage is unacceptable.
Describe password hashing and verifier-side protections.
Identify risky password-policy patterns.

notes.text: Passwords are memorized secrets. Systems should avoid storing them in recoverable form; instead, use a suitable password-hashing approach and a trusted verification API. Modern guidance focuses on password length, screening against known-compromised values, rate limiting, and secure recovery rather than arbitrary complexity rules alone.

Conceptual storage flow:
password -> password hashing function -> stored verifier
login password -> same verifier API -> compare
Never design a custom password-hashing scheme or store reversible password encryption as a substitute for password hashing.

quiz.question: What is the purpose of a password verifier?
options: To compare a supplied password against a securely stored verifier representation
quiz.answer: To compare a supplied password against a securely stored verifier representation
quiz.explanation: Verification should not require recovering the original password.

summary: Password storage should be one-way and resistant to offline guessing.
Secure recovery is part of password security.

lessons.title: Multi-Factor Authentication and Phishing Resistance
lessons.description: Compare OTP, push, hardware, and public-key authenticators with emphasis on phishing resistance.
learningObjectives: Explain why two factors are stronger than one.
Distinguish replay-resistant and phishing-resistant authentication.
Explain why manually entered OTPs are not generally phishing-resistant.

notes.text: NIST SP 800-63B defines phishing resistance as preventing disclosure of authentication secrets or valid authenticator outputs to an impostor verifier without relying on user vigilance. Public-key mechanisms such as WebAuthn can bind credentials to the verifier context.

items: MFA improves security but not all factors resist phishing equally.
Push-based methods can still be abused through fatigue attacks if poorly designed.
Phishing-resistant authenticators should be preferred for high-value access where practical.

practicals.title: Compare MFA Methods
practicals.description: Compare common authentication methods using assurance and phishing-resistance criteria.
steps: Create a comparison table for password-only, OTP MFA, push MFA, and public-key phishing-resistant authentication.
Rate phishing resistance, replay resistance, recovery risk, and operational considerations.
Recommend an approach for a privileged administrator and justify it with NIST assurance concepts.
practicals.solution: A strong recommendation uses phishing-resistant cryptographic authentication for the privileged role where practical, while acknowledging deployment and recovery constraints.
practicals.output: A comparison table plus a short risk-based recommendation.

quiz.question: Which is generally a phishing-resistant approach?
options: A public-key authenticator bound to the verifier context
quiz.answer: A public-key authenticator bound to the verifier context
quiz.explanation: Public-key authenticators can bind authentication to the legitimate verifier.

summary: MFA strength depends on the authenticator and protocol.
Phishing resistance is about the protocol binding, not simply the number of factors.

lessons.title: Account Recovery, Reauthentication, and Session Risk
lessons.description: Secure the pathways used when a user loses a factor or changes a sensitive credential.
learningObjectives: Identify the risks in account-recovery flows.
Explain why sensitive actions may require reauthentication.
Design recovery controls that preserve assurance.

notes.text: Recovery can become the weakest authentication path. Recovery methods should not silently downgrade the security of the account. OWASP recommends context-aware reauthentication for sensitive operations and secure session handling after reauthentication.

items: Avoid knowledge-based questions whose answers are easily discoverable.
Invalidate or rotate affected sessions and credentials after high-risk recovery events.
Require stronger verification when changing authenticators or privileged credentials.

quiz.question: Why should sensitive authenticator changes often trigger reauthentication?
options: Because a compromised active session should not automatically authorize a new high-value authenticator
quiz.answer: Because a compromised active session should not automatically authorize a new high-value authenticator
quiz.explanation: Reauthentication helps protect high-impact changes from session compromise.

summary: Recovery must preserve the intended assurance level.
Session invalidation and token rotation matter after security-sensitive changes.

tasks.title: Create an MFA Assurance Recommendation
tasks.description: Recommend authentication methods for three system roles with different risk levels.
tasks.problemStatement: Choose authentication approaches for a public user, a finance administrator, and a privileged infrastructure administrator. Explain the assurance rationale and recovery requirements.
objectives: Compare authenticators by phishing resistance and assurance.
requirements: NIST SP 800-63B is the primary reference.
Do not claim that any specific vendor product is automatically compliant.
tasks.hint: Prioritize the attack consequences of credential compromise before choosing the authenticator.
tasks.solutionCode:
Role:public-user
Recommended: password plus optional phishing-resistant MFA
Recovery: protected email/second factor with risk controls

Role:finance-admin
Recommended: phishing-resistant MFA
Recovery: stronger verification and admin review

Role:privileged-infrastructure-admin
Recommended: phishing-resistant, replay-resistant cryptographic authentication
Recovery: controlled break-glass process and credential rotation
tasks.solutionExplanation: The recommendation scales authentication strength and recovery controls with privilege and impact, while avoiding unsupported claims about vendor implementations.

modules.title: Authorization and Access Models
modules.description: Design least-privilege authorization using roles, attributes, resource policies, and separation of duties.

lessons.title: Authentication vs Authorization
lessons.description: Make the foundational distinction between proving identity and deciding permissions.
learningObjectives: Explain AuthN versus AuthZ.
Trace an authorization decision through principal, action, resource, and context.
Identify where server-side authorization must be enforced.

notes.text: Authentication answers who or what is acting. Authorization determines whether that principal may perform the requested action on a specific resource in a particular context.

Authorization decision:
principal + action + resource + context -> policy decision
Successful login does not imply access to every object or action in an application.

quiz.question: A logged-in user changes an object identifier and can read another customer's record. What failed?
quiz.answer: Authorization
quiz.explanation: The system failed to enforce whether the authenticated principal was permitted to access that object.

summary: Authentication establishes identity context; authorization must still be evaluated.
Fine-grained decisions often depend on the resource being accessed.

lessons.title: RBAC: Role-Based Access Control
lessons.description: Use roles to express stable job functions without turning roles into uncontrolled permission bundles.
learningObjectives: Explain role and permission relationships.
Design roles with cohesive responsibilities.
Detect role explosion and overly broad roles.

notes.text: RBAC groups permissions around roles such as analyst, reviewer, or administrator. Roles are useful when responsibilities are relatively stable; badly designed roles can become giant bundles of unrelated authority.

items: Use least privilege when mapping permissions into roles.
Prefer narrowly scoped roles over a universal administrator role.
Review role membership and permission contents separately.

quiz.question: What is a common RBAC design problem?
options: Role explosion or overly broad roles
quiz.answer: Role explosion or overly broad roles
quiz.explanation: RBAC quality depends on appropriately scoped roles and maintainable role design.

summary: Roles are abstractions for permissions, not identities themselves.
Good roles align to real responsibilities.

lessons.title: ABAC and Context-Aware Authorization
lessons.description: Model access decisions using attributes and context when roles alone are insufficient.
learningObjectives: Explain attribute-based authorization.
Combine subject, resource, action, and environment attributes.
Design policies that fail closed when required attributes are missing.

notes.text: ABAC evaluates attributes such as department, resource classification, device state, time, or transaction risk. It can express policies that would require many narrowly specialized roles in an RBAC-only design.

Example policy:
allow if subject.department == resource.department
   and resource.classification != "restricted"
   and device.compliant == true
Attribute-based policies depend on trustworthy attribute sources. An attacker who can modify an authorization attribute may influence the decision.

practicals.title: Write an ABAC Policy
practicals.description: Turn subject, resource, and device attributes into a deny-by-default authorization policy.
steps: Define subject.department, resource.classification, action, and device.compliant attributes.
Allow same-department access to non-restricted records only from compliant devices.
Define the deny behavior for missing or invalid attributes.
practicals.solution: ALLOW when subject.department equals resource.department AND resource.classification is not restricted AND device.compliant is true; otherwise DENY.
practicals.output: A policy expression that fails closed when required attributes are absent or untrusted.

quiz.question: Why is ABAC useful when role membership alone is insufficient?
options: It can incorporate resource and context attributes into the decision
quiz.answer: It can incorporate resource and context attributes into the decision
quiz.explanation: ABAC can combine multiple attributes and context signals.

summary: Authorization policy quality depends on trustworthy attributes and explicit deny behavior.
Context can increase precision without creating huge numbers of roles.

lessons.title: Least Privilege and Separation of Duties
lessons.description: Reduce the impact of compromise and insider error by constraining privileges and conflicting duties.
learningObjectives: Apply least privilege to users and services.
Identify toxic combinations of duties.
Explain why separation of duties can require more than one approval or principal.

notes.text: Least privilege gives subjects only the permissions needed for assigned work. Separation of duties reduces fraud or error by ensuring that a sensitive process cannot be completed by one principal alone.

items: Separate request, approval, and execution for high-risk changes where practical.
Apply least privilege to administrators and automation accounts.
Review temporary privileges for scope and expiry.

quiz.question: What does separation of duties primarily reduce?
options: The chance that one principal can complete a sensitive conflicting process alone
quiz.answer: The chance that one principal can complete a sensitive conflicting process alone
quiz.explanation: Separating duties reduces concentrated authority and abuse opportunities.

summary: Least privilege and separation of duties solve different but complementary risks.
Temporary privilege can reduce standing access.

tasks.title: Review an Access Matrix for Toxic Combinations
tasks.description: Analyze a fictional access matrix and identify excessive privileges and separation-of-duties conflicts.
tasks.problemStatement: Given roles for procurement, approval, payment, and reconciliation, identify users who can both initiate and approve the same financial action.
objectives: Detect at least two conflicting permission combinations.
requirements: Present the matrix as CSV, Markdown, or JSON.
tasks.hint: Look for combinations that let one principal initiate, approve, and reconcile the same transaction.
tasks.solutionCode:
Example remediation:
- purchasing users may create purchase orders
- supervisors may approve purchase orders
- finance may release payment
- reconciliation staff may review completed payments
No single role should combine all four capabilities.
tasks.solutionExplanation: The solution breaks a high-risk transaction into distinct authority domains and illustrates separation of duties.

modules.title: Federation and Identity Protocols
modules.description: Understand SAML, OAuth 2.0, OpenID Connect, tokens, and modern federation security patterns.

lessons.title: Identity Federation and Trust Relationships
lessons.description: Understand why federation lets one security domain provide identity information to another.
learningObjectives: Explain identity-provider and relying-party roles.
Describe trust relationships and assertion validation.
Identify federation lifecycle and termination concerns.

notes.text: Federation lets a relying party accept identity information from an identity provider under a defined trust relationship. Trust includes issuer identity, signing keys, endpoints, audience restrictions, and operational agreements.

items: Federation does not remove authorization responsibility from the relying party.
Trust metadata and keys need lifecycle management.
Federation termination must revoke or stop accepting the former trust relationship.

quiz.question: What is a core responsibility of a relying party in a federated system?
options: Validate the assertion and enforce its own authorization rules
quiz.answer: Validate the assertion and enforce its own authorization rules
quiz.explanation: The relying party must validate incoming federation data and still authorize access.

summary: Federation shifts authentication authority, not all authorization responsibility.
Trust relationships require key and metadata management.

lessons.title: SAML 2.0 and Enterprise SSO
lessons.description: Read the major components of SAML-based browser SSO without treating SAML as an authorization protocol.
learningObjectives: Describe IdP, SP, assertion, and audience concepts.
Explain why signing and audience/recipient validation matter.
Recognize SP-initiated and IdP-initiated patterns at a high level.

notes.text: SAML defines a framework for exchanging security information. In browser SSO, an identity provider issues a SAML assertion to a service provider. The service provider should validate the signature, issuer, time conditions, audience, and other relevant constraints before using claims.
A validly signed SAML assertion does not automatically mean the user should receive every permission in the application.

quiz.question: Which SAML property helps prevent an assertion intended for one service from being reused by another?
quiz.answer: Audience restriction
quiz.explanation: Audience checks bind the assertion to the intended relying party context.

summary: SAML is widely used for enterprise federation and browser SSO.
Assertion validation should be strict and policy-driven.

lessons.title: OAuth 2.0: Delegated Authorization
lessons.description: Understand OAuth as an authorization framework for obtaining limited access to HTTP services.
learningObjectives: Identify the roles in OAuth 2.0.
Distinguish access tokens from user authentication.
Explain why scopes should be narrow.

notes.text: OAuth 2.0 enables a client to obtain limited access to an HTTP service. Its core abstraction is delegated authorization. OAuth by itself does not define an end-user identity layer equivalent to OpenID Connect.

Conceptual OAuth roles:
resource owner -> authorizes client
client -> requests access
authorization server -> issues token
resource server -> accepts token
Do not use the presence of an OAuth access token as proof of human identity without validating the identity layer and protocol context.

quiz.question: What is OAuth 2.0 primarily designed to provide?
options: Delegated authorization to access protected resources
quiz.answer: Delegated authorization to access protected resources
quiz.explanation: OAuth defines an authorization framework rather than a password database or firewall.

summary: OAuth access tokens represent delegated authority.
Identity assertions are a separate concern handled by protocols such as OIDC.

lessons.title: OpenID Connect, ID Tokens, and Claims
lessons.description: Use OpenID Connect correctly as an identity layer on OAuth 2.0.
learningObjectives: Explain the role of the ID Token.
Distinguish ID Token claims from access-token authorization scope.
Validate issuer, audience, signature, and nonce/context as appropriate.

notes.text: OpenID Connect adds an identity layer on top of OAuth 2.0. It allows clients to verify the end-user identity based on authentication performed by an authorization server and receive claims about that user.

items: ID Tokens are intended for the client; access tokens are for protected resource access.
Validate token claims and issuer/audience relationships before trusting them.
Nonce and authorization-response binding help defend the authentication flow.

practicals.title: OIDC Token Validation Checklist
practicals.description: Build a protocol-aware checklist for validating identity tokens before trusting claims.
steps: List signature and trusted-key checks.
List issuer and audience checks.
List time-validity checks.
Add nonce or transaction-binding checks when required by the flow.
Write explicit rejection conditions for failed validation.
practicals.solution: Reject invalid signatures, unexpected issuer or audience, expired tokens, and nonce mismatches when nonce is required.
practicals.output: A checklist separating cryptographic validation from semantic and protocol validation.

quiz.question: Which token is specifically defined by OIDC to convey identity claims to the client?
quiz.answer: ID Token
quiz.explanation: OIDC defines the ID Token as the identity layer artifact.

summary: OIDC adds authentication semantics to OAuth.
Token validation is part of relying-party security.

tasks.title: Choose SAML, OAuth 2.0, or OIDC
tasks.description: Select the appropriate protocol for three federation scenarios.
tasks.problemStatement: Choose between SAML SSO, OAuth 2.0 delegated authorization, and OpenID Connect authentication for three architecture cases. Explain what the selected protocol does and what it does not do.
objectives: Identify the principal security validation steps.
requirements: Use the protocol standards linked in the lesson resources.
tasks.hint: Ask first whether the requirement is SSO/federation, delegated API authorization, or user authentication.
tasks.solutionCode:
Scenario A: Enterprise browser SSO -> SAML
Scenario B: Mobile client needs scoped API access -> OAuth 2.0
Scenario C: Web application needs user sign-in and identity claims -> OpenID Connect
tasks.solutionExplanation: The mapping is based on protocol purpose: federation/SSO, delegated resource authorization, and identity on top of OAuth respectively.

modules.title: Provisioning, Directory Services, and Access Automation
modules.description: Manage identity data and access changes across directories and applications with reliable automation.

lessons.title: Directory Services and Group Management
lessons.description: Understand directory concepts, group nesting, and authoritative identity attributes.
learningObjectives: Explain directory users, groups, and attributes.
Identify risks from nested groups and uncontrolled membership.
Separate identity-source authority from application-local roles.

notes.text: Directory services provide centralized identity and group information. Applications may map groups or attributes into local roles, but the mapping should be explicit and reviewed.

items: Nested groups can create surprising transitive privilege.
Protect authoritative attributes from unauthorized modification.
Avoid using one directory group to represent unrelated business and technical permissions.

quiz.question: What is a common security problem with deeply nested groups?
options: Transitive membership can create unexpected privilege
quiz.answer: Transitive membership can create unexpected privilege
quiz.explanation: Nested membership can make effective authorization difficult to reason about.

summary: Group design should remain understandable and auditable.
Effective access must account for inherited membership.

lessons.title: SCIM and Lifecycle Provisioning
lessons.description: Use SCIM concepts to automate account and group provisioning between identity systems and applications.
learningObjectives: Explain SCIM as a provisioning protocol.
Describe create, update, disable, and group-membership synchronization.
Identify idempotency and error-handling concerns in provisioning workflows.

notes.text: SCIM standardizes HTTP-based provisioning of identity resources such as Users and Groups. Provisioning integrations should cope with retries, partial failures, duplicate requests, and out-of-order lifecycle events.

Provisioning flow:
HR/authoritative source -> IdP -> SCIM service -> application identity store
Provisioning success does not prove authorization correctness. The target application still needs safe role mapping and enforcement.

practicals.title: SCIM Reconciliation Exercise
practicals.description: Find provisioning drift between an authoritative identity source and an application target.
steps: Create a fictional source list and target list.
Match identities using a stable identifier.
Classify missing, changed, duplicate, stale, and identical records.
Assign a safe reconciliation action to each difference.
practicals.solution: Missing target record -> create; changed attributes -> update; stale target status -> disable or update to match source; duplicate stable identifiers -> manual review; identical records -> no-op.
practicals.output: A deterministic reconciliation table covering every source-target difference.

quiz.question: What is a key benefit of SCIM?
quiz.answer: Standardized identity provisioning between systems
quiz.explanation: SCIM provides a standard way to provision identity resources across systems.

summary: SCIM improves lifecycle interoperability.
Provisioning integrations need retry and reconciliation strategies.

lessons.title: Access Requests, Approvals, and Reconciliation
lessons.description: Design a controlled access-request workflow and periodic reconciliation.
learningObjectives: Model request, approval, provisioning, review, and revocation states.
Explain reconciliation against authoritative access records.
Identify drift between intended and effective access.

items: Requests should identify requested resource, action, duration, and business purpose.
Approvals should come from an accountable owner.
Reconciliation compares intended grants with actual technical state.
Temporary access should have an explicit expiry.

notes.text:
State model:
requested -> approved -> provisioned -> reviewed -> revoked/expired

quiz.question: What does reconciliation primarily detect?
options: Differences between intended access and actual technical state
quiz.answer: Differences between intended access and actual technical state
quiz.explanation: Reconciliation looks for access drift and synchronization failures.

summary: Access workflows need traceability across request and technical enforcement.
Reconciliation is necessary even when provisioning is automated.

lessons.title: Deprovisioning, Orphaned Accounts, and Token Revocation
lessons.description: Make access removal reliable across accounts, sessions, groups, and application credentials.
learningObjectives: Identify deprovisioning failure modes.
Describe token/session revocation considerations.
Create a containment checklist for a high-risk identity departure.

notes.text: Disabling a primary account may not remove downstream sessions, API tokens, group memberships, local accounts, or application-specific credentials. Effective deprovisioning therefore needs both identity-provider actions and target-system cleanup.

items: Track high-value application sessions and refresh tokens.
Remove privileged group memberships promptly.
Rotate or revoke non-human credentials owned by the departing operator when appropriate.

quiz.question: Why may disabling an identity account be insufficient on its own?
options: Existing sessions, tokens, or downstream accounts may remain active
quiz.answer: Existing sessions, tokens, or downstream accounts may remain active
quiz.explanation: Deprovisioning must address active and delegated credentials beyond the primary account.

summary: Deprovisioning is a distributed control problem.
Credential and session inventories improve response speed.

tasks.title: Design a SCIM Reconciliation Strategy
tasks.description: Create a reconciliation plan for a provisioning integration.
tasks.problemStatement: Define how to detect and resolve duplicates, failed updates, stale accounts, and membership drift between an IdP and application.
objectives: Define a reconciliation schedule or trigger.
Define safe retry and manual-review conditions.
tasks.hint: Keep the authoritative identity identifier separate from a mutable display name.
tasks.solutionCode:
Reconciliation outline:
1. Pull authoritative users by stable external identifier.
2. Compare target records by that identifier.
3. Queue missing/changed records for deterministic update.
4. Flag duplicate identifiers for manual review.
5. Mark stale target records for disable/revocation workflow.
6. Emit an audit record for every correction.
tasks.solutionExplanation: The strategy uses stable identifiers, deterministic comparison, explicit duplicate handling, and auditability.

modules.title: Privileged Access and Non-Human Identities
modules.description: Protect administrator access, service identities, workload credentials, and emergency paths.

lessons.title: Privileged Access Management Concepts
lessons.description: Reduce standing administrative exposure and improve accountability.
learningObjectives: Explain standing privilege versus just-in-time privilege.
Design privileged account separation.
Identify approval, monitoring, and expiry controls for high-risk access.

notes.text: Privileged access management limits the blast radius of administrative credentials. Common patterns include separate admin identities, just-in-time elevation, session monitoring, approval, and strong authentication.

items: Use ordinary accounts for routine work and separate privileged identities for administration.
Limit elevation duration and scope.
Monitor privileged operations and retain evidence appropriate to policy.

practicals.title: Privileged Access Review
practicals.description: Identify standing administrative privilege and design safer elevation controls.
steps: Review a fictional administrator access list.
Identify assignments without expiry, recent review, or documented purpose.
Replace unnecessary standing privilege with time-bound elevation where appropriate.
Define monitoring and post-use review.
practicals.solution: Use separate privileged identities, strong authentication, time-bound elevation, approval, activity logging, and a controlled emergency path.

quiz.question: What is the main advantage of just-in-time privilege?
options: It reduces the duration of standing administrative authority
It removes the need for authentication
quiz.answer: It reduces the duration of standing administrative authority
quiz.explanation: Temporary privilege reduces persistent exposure.

summary: Privileged access deserves stronger controls than routine access.
JIT access does not replace authorization or monitoring.

lessons.title: Service Accounts and Workload Identity
lessons.description: Secure identities used by applications, jobs, and services.
learningObjectives: Explain why static service credentials are risky.
Identify workload-identity patterns.
Apply least privilege and credential rotation principles to non-human identities.

notes.text: Non-human identities often outlive individual people and may operate with powerful permissions. Prefer short-lived or platform-managed credentials where supported, minimize permissions, and assign accountable owners.
Do not hard-code long-lived production credentials in source repositories or deployment manifests.

quiz.question: Which design most reduces the exposure of a long-lived service credential?
options: Use a short-lived or platform-issued workload credential with narrowly scoped permissions
Put the same password in every service
Store the credential in source code
quiz.answer: Use a short-lived or platform-issued workload credential with narrowly scoped permissions
quiz.explanation: Shorter-lived, scoped credentials reduce blast radius and persistence.

summary: Non-human identities need owners, inventory, and lifecycle controls.
Prefer workload identity over static shared secrets where supported.

lessons.title: Secrets, Keys, and Credential Rotation
lessons.description: Establish secure handling and rotation processes for identity secrets and keys.
learningObjectives: Distinguish password verifiers, API secrets, signing keys, and encryption keys.
Describe safe secret storage.
Plan rotation and compromise response.

items: Store secrets in protected secret-management systems or platform mechanisms appropriate to the environment.
Separate key access from application data access where practical.
Rotation without revocation can fail if old credentials remain valid.
Compromise response should include scope assessment and rotation/revocation.

notes.text: Do not log passwords, access tokens, private keys, or other authentication secrets.

quiz.question: What is a weakness of rotating a secret without revoking the old credential when supported?
options: The old credential may remain usable
quiz.answer: The old credential may remain usable
quiz.explanation: Rotation must ensure previous credentials are invalidated where the system supports it.

summary: Credential lifecycle includes creation, storage, use, rotation, and revocation.
Secret management should be integrated with incident response.

lessons.title: Break-Glass and Emergency Access
lessons.description: Design emergency access that is available when normal identity systems fail but remains heavily controlled.
learningObjectives: Explain when emergency access is justified.
Design safeguards around emergency credentials.
Specify logging, notification, review, and post-use rotation.

notes.text: Emergency access exists for exceptional conditions such as identity-provider outages. It should be rare, tightly controlled, monitored, and reviewed after use.

items: Use separate credentials and storage controls.
Alert when emergency credentials are used.
Rotate or replace credentials after use where appropriate.
Test the process periodically without creating unnecessary routine use.

quiz.question: What should normally happen after an emergency privileged credential is used?
options: Post-use review and credential rotation/replacement as appropriate
The credential should become the routine admin account
All other admin accounts should be disabled
quiz.answer: Post-use review and credential rotation/replacement as appropriate
quiz.explanation: Emergency use should trigger review and restoration of the intended secure state.

summary: Break-glass access is an exception, not a convenience path.
Operational resilience requires testing the emergency procedure.

tasks.title: Create a Privileged Access Design
tasks.description: Design privileged access for infrastructure administrators without relying on permanent broad admin rights.
tasks.problemStatement: Define normal identity, privileged identity, elevation, approval, session monitoring, and emergency access patterns for a fictional infrastructure team.
requirements: Use least privilege and separation of duties.
Avoid depending on one vendor product.
tasks.hint: Create separate paths for routine work, approved elevation, and emergency recovery.
tasks.solutionCode:
Design:
- normal account: email, documentation, non-admin work
- privileged account: separate identity, phishing-resistant MFA
- elevation: approved, time-bound role assignment
- monitoring: privileged activity logged centrally
- emergency: protected break-glass credential, alert on use, post-use rotation
tasks.solutionExplanation: The design reduces standing privilege while maintaining a resilient emergency path and strong attribution.

modules.title: Sessions, Tokens, and Access Enforcement
modules.description: Protect web sessions, bearer tokens, and application authorization boundaries.

lessons.title: Session Management Fundamentals
lessons.description: Understand how applications maintain authenticated state across requests.
learningObjectives: Explain session identifiers and server-side session state.
Identify session fixation and theft risks.
Apply secure session lifecycle concepts.

notes.text: HTTP is stateless, so applications use session mechanisms to associate subsequent requests with an authenticated principal. The session identifier effectively represents the authenticated state and therefore requires strong protection.

items: Generate unpredictable session identifiers.
Regenerate or rotate identifiers after authentication or privilege changes where appropriate.
Expire sessions according to risk and user expectations.

quiz.question: Why should session identifiers be treated as sensitive?
options: They can represent the authenticated session and its associated authorization
quiz.answer: They can represent the authenticated session and its associated authorization
quiz.explanation: A stolen session identifier may allow use of the active session.

summary: Session security is part of authentication security.
Protect session identifiers as carefully as other authenticators.

lessons.title: Cookies and Browser Session Controls
lessons.description: Use Secure, HttpOnly, SameSite, and related controls appropriately.
learningObjectives: Explain Secure, HttpOnly, and SameSite cookie attributes.
Select cookie behavior for cross-site requirements.
Identify cookie scope risks.

notes.text: Set-Cookie: session=opaque-id; Secure; HttpOnly; SameSite=Lax; Path=/

items: Secure limits transmission to HTTPS connections.
HttpOnly prevents direct JavaScript access through document.cookie in supporting browsers.
SameSite controls cross-site cookie sending behavior.
Domain and Path should be as narrow as practical.

quiz.question: Which cookie attribute primarily prevents JavaScript from reading a session cookie?
quiz.answer: HttpOnly
quiz.explanation: HttpOnly restricts document.cookie access from scripts.

summary: Cookie settings are defense in depth; they do not replace authorization.
Cross-site application requirements should be considered when selecting SameSite behavior.

lessons.title: Bearer Tokens, JWTs, and Validation
lessons.description: Understand the security properties and pitfalls of bearer access tokens and JWTs.
learningObjectives: Explain why bearer tokens need protection in transit and storage.
Describe JWT signature and claim validation.
Identify risks from accepting tokens without issuer/audience/algorithm checks.

notes.text: A bearer token grants authority to whoever possesses it. JWT is a token format, not an authorization policy. Signed JWTs can carry claims, but consumers still need to validate signature, issuer, audience, time, and relevant application-specific claims.
Do not accept a JWT merely because it is syntactically valid or decodes successfully.

quiz.question: Why is decoding a JWT not sufficient validation?
options: Decoding does not prove the signature, issuer, audience, or validity constraints
quiz.answer: Decoding does not prove the signature, issuer, audience, or validity constraints
quiz.explanation: A token must be cryptographically and semantically validated.

summary: Token format and token security are separate concerns.
Bearer tokens increase the importance of secure storage and transmission.

lessons.title: Authorization Enforcement at Resource Boundaries
lessons.description: Apply object-level and action-level authorization consistently across APIs and services.
learningObjectives: Design authorization checks around resource ownership or permissions.
Prevent insecure direct object reference patterns.
Use centralized policy logic without bypassing resource-specific decisions.

notes.text:
Request:
GET /accounts/482

Server checks:
1. authenticate caller
2. load account 482
3. authorize caller for account 482
4. return only permitted fields
Client-side route hiding or UI checks are not security boundaries. The server that owns the resource must enforce authorization.

quiz.question: Where should access to a protected resource ultimately be enforced?
options: At the server/resource boundary that controls the resource
quiz.answer: At the server/resource boundary that controls the resource
quiz.explanation: The authoritative resource server must enforce authorization.

summary: Resource ownership and permission checks belong at the enforcement point.
UI restrictions can improve UX but do not establish security.

tasks.title: Review a Token Validation Checklist
tasks.description: Build a checklist for validating an OIDC ID Token or JWT-like signed assertion before trusting its identity claims.
tasks.problemStatement: Create a checklist that covers signature, algorithm policy, issuer, audience, time claims, nonce/context when applicable, and error handling.
objectives: Distinguish cryptographic validation from semantic validation.
Explain why token decoding is not enough.
requirements: Use OIDC/JWT references from the lesson.
tasks.hint: Think in two layers: cryptographic validity and protocol/application validity.
tasks.solutionCode:
Checklist:
- verify signature with trusted key
- restrict accepted algorithms
- verify issuer
- verify audience
- verify time validity
- verify nonce/state binding when the flow requires it
- reject malformed or ambiguous inputs
- log a safe validation failure without exposing token contents
tasks.solutionExplanation: The checklist separates trust in the signing material from the protocol context in which the token is accepted.

modules.title: Identity Governance, Monitoring, and Zero Trust
modules.description: Turn IAM into a continuously reviewed security capability using access reviews, policy engines, and identity telemetry.

lessons.title: Access Reviews and Certification
lessons.description: Design periodic review of high-risk access and role memberships.
learningObjectives: Explain the purpose of access certification.
Prioritize reviews by risk and privilege.
Define evidence for approve/revoke decisions.

notes.text: Access reviews validate whether current access remains justified. A useful certification process gives reviewers the context needed to make a decision and records the decision and resulting action.

items: Prioritize privileged and sensitive access.
Make reviewers accountable for business context.
Separate certification from automatic renewal when possible.

quiz.question: What is the primary objective of an access review?
options: Confirm that current access remains justified and appropriate
quiz.answer: Confirm that current access remains justified and appropriate
quiz.explanation: Reviews detect stale or unjustified access.

summary: Certification closes the loop on lifecycle drift.
High-risk access deserves more frequent or deeper review.

lessons.title: Identity Monitoring and Detection Signals
lessons.description: Detect suspicious authentication and privilege behavior using identity telemetry.
learningObjectives: Identify high-value identity events.
Design simple detection hypotheses.
Correlate login, device, location, and privilege-change signals.

items: High-value telemetry may include authentication outcomes, MFA changes, group membership changes, privileged role activation, token issuance, and recovery events.
Detections should distinguish expected maintenance from suspicious behavior.
Centralized logging improves correlation across identity systems and applications.

notes.text: Avoid treating one anomalous login signal as proof of compromise; scope and corroborating evidence matter.

practicals.title: Identity Monitoring Detection Exercise
practicals.description: Design a detection for unexpected privileged-role activation.
steps: Define the event source and required context fields.
State normal administration behavior.
Define suspicious patterns such as missing approval context or unusual timing.
Write a triage checklist to validate the event.
practicals.solution: Alert on privileged-role activation that lacks expected approval context or occurs outside the documented administration window; validate the activity before escalating.
practicals.output: A detection hypothesis and analyst triage checklist.

quiz.question: Which identity event is particularly useful for privileged-access monitoring?
quiz.answer: Unexpected privileged-role activation
quiz.explanation: Privilege changes can materially alter what an identity can do.

summary: Identity monitoring should focus on events that change trust or authority.
Detection quality improves when identity events are correlated with context.

lessons.title: Zero Trust and Identity-Centric Access
lessons.description: Apply zero-trust principles to identity, device, application, and resource decisions.
learningObjectives: Explain why network location is insufficient as a trust signal.
Describe identity-centric and resource-centric policy decisions.
Relate least privilege to zero-trust architecture.

notes.text: NIST SP 800-207 describes zero trust as avoiding implicit trust based solely on network location and focusing policy decisions on users, assets, resources, and context.

items: Authenticate and authorize before access to protected resources.
Use device and contextual signals when they materially improve the decision.
Continuously evaluate access in systems where risk can change during a session.

quiz.question: Which statement best matches zero-trust architecture?
options: Trust is automatically granted to anything on the internal network
Network location alone is not sufficient to establish trust
quiz.answer: Network location alone is not sufficient to establish trust
quiz.explanation: Zero trust removes implicit trust based solely on network position.

summary: Zero trust is an architectural strategy, not one product.
Identity and resource policy are central decision inputs.

lessons.title: Conditional Access and Contextual Policy
lessons.description: Use conditional policy concepts to express identity-aware access requirements.
learningObjectives: Model if-then access policies.
Choose signals such as user, device, application, or risk.
Explain why staged testing is important for deny/block policies.

notes.text: Conditional access uses contextual signals to decide whether to allow, require stronger authentication, restrict access, or block a request. Microsoft Entra documentation describes conditions and grant/block controls and recommends report-only testing for policy changes.

Conceptual rule:
IF privileged_user AND unmanaged_device
THEN require strong authentication or block
A poorly scoped block policy can lock out legitimate administrators. Stage and test high-impact policy changes before broad enforcement.

quiz.question: Why is staged testing important for conditional-access block policies?
options: An overly broad policy can unintentionally deny legitimate access
quiz.answer: An overly broad policy can unintentionally deny legitimate access
quiz.explanation: Block policies can have wide operational impact and should be tested carefully.

summary: Context-aware access is policy engineering, not just feature activation.
Report-only modes and what-if analysis can reduce rollout risk.

tasks.title: Build an Identity Detection Use-Case Set
tasks.description: Create four detection use cases centered on identity compromise and privilege abuse.
tasks.problemStatement: Define detections for suspicious MFA-factor changes, impossible-to-explain sign-in context, privileged-role activation outside expected windows, and account-recovery abuse.
objectives: Define triage evidence and false-positive considerations.
requirements: Use identity events rather than generic malware detections.
Do not claim geolocation certainty from a single IP address.
tasks.hint: For each use case specify signal, context, expected behavior, suspicious behavior, and analyst action.
tasks.solutionCode:
Use case: unexpected MFA change
Signals: factor-registration event + identity + time
Triage: verify change request, device context, recent recovery

Use case: privileged role activation outside expected window
Signals: role activation + identity + time + ticket reference
Triage: validate authorized change, inspect related activity
tasks.solutionExplanation: The design ties detections to identity-state changes and provides an analyst path rather than simply labeling the event malicious.

modules.title: Final Real-World Project — IAM Access Governance Analyzer
modules.description: Final assessment combining identity lifecycle, authorization, privileged access, access review, and defensive automation concepts. No module tasks are included in the capstone module.

lessons.title: Capstone Design and Control Mapping
lessons.description: Translate IAM requirements into a small auditable analysis application.
learningObjectives: Map IAM controls to deterministic analysis rules.
Define inputs, outputs, assumptions, and safe operational boundaries.
Create acceptance criteria before implementation.

notes.text: The capstone is deliberately read-only. It analyzes an exported identity/access dataset and identifies governance gaps. A real deployment would need authoritative data sources, stronger policy integration, access controls, and organization-specific approvals.

items: Each finding category must have a clear rationale.
The report should contain enough evidence for a reviewer to investigate further.
The tool must not silently modify identity state.

quiz.question: Why is the capstone read-only?
options: To preserve an explicit separation between analysis and account-changing actions
Because identity systems never allow changes
quiz.answer: To preserve an explicit separation between analysis and account-changing actions
quiz.explanation: The course focuses on evidence-based governance while avoiding unsafe real-system modification.

summary: Good security automation is predictable, scoped, and auditable.
Control findings should map back to IAM objectives.

lessons.title: Capstone Validation and Operational Review
lessons.description: Test the project and evaluate whether its findings are useful and explainable.
learningObjectives: Run syntax and automated tests.
Interpret findings without overclaiming compromise.
Identify limitations and safe next improvements.

notes.text:
Validation commands:
python -m py_compile iam_audit.py
python -m pytest -q
python iam_audit.py data.json
Passing unit tests demonstrates the tested requirements, not universal correctness for every identity system.

quiz.question: What is an appropriate limitation to document for the capstone?
options: It operates on a local export and cannot prove the live state of an external identity system
It can never detect any finding
quiz.answer: It operates on a local export and cannot prove the live state of an external identity system
quiz.explanation: Documenting scope and limitations is part of trustworthy security engineering.

summary: Validate both code behavior and analytical limitations.
A governance finding is an investigation lead, not automatically proof of abuse.

project.name: IAM Access Governance Analyzer
project.description: Build a local, read-only analyzer that turns a small identity/access export into actionable governance findings. The project combines account lifecycle thinking, role-based access, MFA coverage, separation of duties, access reviews, structured reporting, and automated testing.
steps: Create a local project directory and place the supplied data.json beside the analyzer.
Implement strict JSON shape validation for the expected users array.
Evaluate disabled identities that still carry role assignments.
Flag privileged identities that lack MFA.
Detect role combinations that violate documented separation-of-duties rules.
Flag reviews older than the configured review period.
Produce a structured JSON report containing counts, highest severity, findings, and safe next-step recommendations.
Run automated tests for normal findings and privileged-account MFA coverage.
Keep the application read-only; do not connect to real identity providers or modify accounts.

code.README.md:
# IAM Access Governance Analyzer

A local, defensive training application that analyzes a JSON export of identities,
roles, permissions, and review metadata. It reports stale identities, excessive
role assignments, missing MFA for privileged users, and simple separation-of-duties conflicts.

The tool is read-only: it never changes accounts or access.
code.test_iam_audit.py:
import json
import subprocess
import sys
from pathlib import Path

ROOT = Path(__file__).resolve().parent

def test_detects_expected_findings():
    result = subprocess.run(
        [sys.executable, str(ROOT / "iam_audit.py"), str(ROOT / "data.json"), "--review-days", "180"],
        capture_output=True, text=True, check=True
    )
    report = json.loads(result.stdout)
    categories = {item["category"] for item in report["findings"]}
    assert "disabled_with_access" in categories
    assert "privileged_without_mfa" not in categories
    assert "sod_conflict" in categories

def test_mfa_finding():
    doc = {
        "users":[{"id":"x","status":"active","roles":["admin"],"mfa":False,"last_review":"2026-09-01"}],
        "role_permissions":{"admin":["role.manage"]},
        "sod_conflicts":[]
    }
    path = ROOT / "mfa.json"
    path.write_text(json.dumps(doc), encoding="utf-8")
    try:
        result = subprocess.run([sys.executable, str(ROOT / "iam_audit.py"), str(path)], capture_output=True, text=True, check=True)
        report = json.loads(result.stdout)
        assert any(f["category"] == "privileged_without_mfa" for f in report["findings"])
    finally:
        path.unlink()

project.explanation: The capstone uses a deterministic analysis pipeline: identity/access export -> input validation -> governance rules -> severity aggregation -> report. Each rule maps to an IAM control objective taught earlier. The application does not disable users or change roles; this is deliberate so students learn to distinguish analysis from authorized change execution. The tests verify both expected findings and an explicit privileged-MFA rule, giving students a repeatable baseline for extending the analyzer safely.
